pos: n. phrase (the believer's ordinary conduct under the Spirit's government; Paul's command in Galatians 5 and its description in Romans 8)
etymology: Two Greek verbs lie behind the one English word. Peripateo, to walk about, is the New Testament's usual word for how a man conducts his life; stoicheo, in Galatians 5:25, is to walk in line, to keep step in a rank — a soldier's word.
biblical_def: To walk in the Spirit is commanded with a promise attached: “This I say then, Walk in the Spirit, and ye shall not fulfil the lust of the flesh” (Gal 5:16). The conflict is normal: “the flesh lusteth against the Spirit, and the Spirit against the flesh: and these are contrary the one to the other: so that ye cannot do the things that ye would” (Gal 5:17). The output is fruit rather than effort: “the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, longsuffering, gentleness, goodness, faith” (Gal 5:22). The command is repeated with a different verb: “If we live in the Spirit, let us also walk in the Spirit” (Gal 5:25). And Romans makes it the mark of those in whom the law is fulfilled: “who walk not after the flesh, but after the Spirit” (Rom 8:4).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines walk, figuratively, as to move or go on, to behave, to pursue a particular course of life, and, in Scripture, to live and act or behave; and to walk in the Spirit as to live under the influence and direction of the Holy Spirit.
webster_full: WALK, v.i. To move slowly on the feet; to step slowly along.
4. To be in motion; to act; to move; to conduct oneself; to pursue a particular course of life.
5. In Scripture, to live and act or behave; to pursue a particular course of life.
To walk in the flesh, to live and act according to the corrupt propensities of the flesh.
To walk in the Spirit, to live and act under the influence and direction of the Holy Spirit.
scriptures: Gal 5:16
This I say then, Walk in the Spirit, and ye shall not fulfil the lust of the flesh.
Gal 5:17
For the flesh lusteth against the Spirit, and the Spirit against the flesh: and these are contrary the one to the other: so that ye cannot do the things that ye would.
Gal 5:22
But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, longsuffering, gentleness, goodness, faith,
Gal 5:25
If we live in the Spirit, let us also walk in the Spirit.
Rom 8:4
That the righteousness of the law might be fulfilled in us, who walk not after the flesh, but after the Spirit.
corruption_summary: Walking in the Spirit is imagined as an elevated state above the conflict, and Paul describes it as the conflict itself, walked through.
corruption_paragraphs: Galatians 5:17 is the verse that dismantles the elevated-state reading, and it is often skipped between the command in 16 and the fruit in 22. The flesh lusteth against the Spirit, and the Spirit against the flesh, and these are contrary the one to the other, so that ye cannot do the things that ye would. That is written to people who are walking in the Spirit, as a description of what it is like. The believer who feels the pull of the flesh and is troubled by it is not failing to walk in the Spirit; the trouble is the Spirit's opposition being felt. A man in whom there is no struggle has one party absent.

The two verbs correct two opposite errors. Peripateo in verse 16 is the ordinary word for conduct — how a man walks about, buys, speaks, works, keeps his temper — so the walk is not a devotional exercise but a whole life, and there is no walking in the Spirit that is not visible on Tuesday. Stoicheo in verse 25 is to keep step in line, and it corrects the opposite drift toward a purely private spirituality: the Spirit sets the pace and the direction, and the believer's part is not to lead but to keep rank, which is the humbler and harder thing.

The passage's most important word is fruit, set against the works of the flesh in verse 19. Works are manufactured; fruit grows. A congregation that treats love, joy, peace and the rest as targets to be hit by effort has turned Galatians back into the law Paul wrote it to refute. The command is to walk — to keep going in the Spirit's company and under His direction — and the fruit is what appears on a life so walked, over time, by a process the walker does not control. Romans 8:4 says the righteousness of the law is fulfilled in such people, which is a passive, and deliberately so.
roots_summary: Greek peripateo (G4043), to walk about, conduct oneself; stoicheo (G4748), to walk in line, keep step; epithumeo (G1937), to lust, desire; karpos (G2590), fruit.
roots_lines: Greek pneumati peripateite (G4043) — walk in the Spirit; Galatians 5:16; the same verb, Romans 8:4, Ephesians 4:1, Colossians 1:10.
Greek pneumati stoichomen (G4748) — let us keep step in the Spirit; Galatians 5:25, 6:16, Romans 4:12, Philippians 3:16.
Greek karpos tou pneumatos (G2590) — the fruit of the Spirit; Galatians 5:22 — singular fruit, nine qualities.
usage: “So that ye cannot do the things that ye would” — written to people walking in the Spirit.
“Let us also walk in the Spirit” — and the second verb means keep step.
“The fruit of the Spirit” — fruit grows; works are manufactured.

pos: n. phrase (the wilderness miracle at Horeb and again at Kadesh; Paul's type of Christ, the Rock that followed them)
etymology: Two Hebrew words for the rock: tsur at Horeb in Exodus 17, sela at Kadesh in Numbers 20 — a crag rather than a boulder. The places were named Massah and Meribah, testing and strife, after what the people did there.
biblical_def: Water from the rock is given at Horeb by a blow: “Behold, I will stand before thee there upon the rock in Horeb; and thou shalt smite the rock, and there shall come water out of it, that the people may drink” (Exo 17:6). At Kadesh the instruction changes: “Take the rod… and speak ye unto the rock before their eyes; and it shall give forth his water” (Num 20:8). Moses strikes instead: “with his rod he smote the rock twice: and the water came out abundantly” (Num 20:11). The sentence follows: “Because ye believed me not, to sanctify me in the eyes of the children of Israel, therefore ye shall not bring this congregation into the land” (Num 20:12). And Paul names the Rock: “they drank of that spiritual Rock that followed them: and that Rock was Christ” (1Co 10:4).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines rock as a large mass of stony matter, and, in Scripture, figuratively, defense, means of safety, protection, asylum; and smite as to strike, to give a blow with the hand or an instrument.
webster_full: ROCK, n. A large mass of stony matter, usually compounded of two or more simple minerals, either bedded in the earth or resting on its surface.
2. In Scripture, figuratively, defense; means of safety; protection; strength; asylum.
SMITE, v.t. To strike; to throw, drive or force against, as the fist or hand, a stone or a weapon.
2. To kill; to destroy the life of by beating or by weapons of any kind.
4. To strike or affect with passion.
scriptures: Exo 17:6

Behold, I will stand before thee there upon the rock in Horeb; and thou shalt smite the rock, and there shall come water out of it, that the people may drink. And Moses did so in the sight of the elders of Israel.
Num 20:8

Take the rod, and gather thou the assembly together, thou, and Aaron thy brother, and speak ye unto the rock before their eyes; and it shall give forth his water, and thou shalt bring forth to them water out of the rock: so thou shalt give the congregation and their beasts drink.
And Moses lifted up his hand, and with his rod he smote the rock twice: and the water came out abundantly, and the congregation drank, and their beasts also.

And the LORD spake unto Moses and Aaron, Because ye believed me not, to sanctify me in the eyes of the children of Israel, therefore ye shall not bring this congregation into the land which I have given them.
And did all drink the same spiritual drink: for they drank of that spiritual Rock that followed them: and that Rock was Christ.
corruption_summary: Moses' punishment looks disproportionate, and the text says what he did: he misrepresented God in public, and struck what was to be spoken to.
corruption_paragraphs: Numbers 20 troubles readers because the water came anyway, abundantly, and the man who had led Israel forty years lost the land over a rod. The verse gives the charge and it is not a rod: because ye believed me not, to sanctify me in the eyes of the children of Israel. Moses had said, must we fetch you water out of this rock? — we — and had struck in anger what God had told him to address in speech, before the whole congregation. A leader's public misrepresentation of God is judged by a stricter measure, and James 3:1 says so for teachers in the church: the greater condemnation. The severity is the doctrine of office.

The Reformed have also read the change of instruction typologically, and the reading is old and sober rather than fanciful. Paul says the Rock was Christ. At Horeb the Rock was struck, and water came; at Kadesh it was to be spoken to, and would give its water on a word. Christ is smitten once — Hebrews insists on the once — and thereafter His people come to Him by asking. Moses struck the Rock a second time, and twice, and the type was broken in the sight of everyone. Whether or not that reading is pressed, it is at least clear that the two miracles were meant to be different, and Moses made them the same.

Exodus 17:6 contains the line that turns the story from a miracle into a gospel: I will stand before thee there upon the rock. The LORD positions Himself on the rock that is about to be struck. Paul's that Rock was Christ is the fulfilment of that image — the blow that brought the water fell where God had chosen to stand. And the water followed them; 1 Corinthians 10:4 says so, and it is the same chapter that warns that with many of them God was not well pleased, for they were overthrown in the wilderness. Drinking from the Rock is not the same as entering the land.
roots_summary: Hebrew tsur (H6697), a rock; sela (H5553), a crag; nakah (H5221), to smite; Meribah (H4809), strife; Greek petra (G4073), rock.
roots_lines: Hebrew tsur (H6697) — the rock at Horeb; Exodus 17:6, Deuteronomy 8:15, Psalm 78:20, 105:41.
Hebrew sela (H5553) — the crag at Kadesh; Numbers 20:8–11, Nehemiah 9:15, Psalm 78:16.
Greek pneumatikes petras (G4152, G4073) — that spiritual Rock; 1 Corinthians 10:4.
usage: “I will stand before thee there upon the rock” — God positioned where the blow would fall.
“Speak ye unto the rock” — and he smote it twice.
“That Rock was Christ” — and the same chapter says many were overthrown.

pos: n. phrase (the panoplia of Ephesians 6 — the complete equipment God supplies for standing against the devil)
etymology: Greek panoplia, from pan, all, and hopla, arms — the full kit of a heavily armed infantryman. Paul wrote it chained to one, and the pieces he lists are the ones he would have looked at every day. The AV spells it armour.
biblical_def: The whole armour of God is issued with its purpose stated: “Put on the whole armour of God, that ye may be able to stand against the wiles of the devil” (Eph 6:11), and again, “that ye may be able to withstand in the evil day, and having done all, to stand” (Eph 6:13). Its one weapon is named last: “take the helmet of salvation, and the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God” (Eph 6:17). Romans calls the same kit by another name: “let us therefore cast off the works of darkness, and let us put on the armour of light” (Rom 13:12). And Thessalonians issues a shorter version: “putting on the breastplate of faith and love; and for an helmet, the hope of salvation” (1Th 5:8).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines armor as defensive arms; any habit worn to protect the body in battle; and, figuratively, in Scripture, the whole armor of God as the Christian graces and means of defense against spiritual enemies.
webster_full: ARMOR, n. Defensive arms; any habit worn to protect the body in battle; formerly called harness.
It was usually made of metal, and consisted of a helmet, a breastplate, greaves, and other pieces.
2. In a spiritual sense, the Christian graces and means of defense and offense against spiritual enemies; as the armor of God.
PANOPLY, n. Complete armor or defense.
scriptures: Eph 6:11
Put on the whole armour of God, that ye may be able to stand against the wiles of the devil.
Eph 6:13
Wherefore take unto you the whole armour of God, that ye may be able to withstand in the evil day, and having done all, to stand.
Eph 6:17
And take the helmet of salvation, and the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God:
The night is far spent, the day is at hand: let us therefore cast off the works of darkness, and let us put on the armour of light.
But let us, who are of the day, be sober, putting on the breastplate of faith and love; and for an helmet, the hope of salvation.
corruption_summary: The pieces are preached as techniques the believer performs, and every piece is a thing God is or gives, and Isaiah shows Him wearing it first.
corruption_paragraphs: The armour is of God, and the genitive is doing more than most sermons allow. Isaiah 59:17 shows the LORD Himself putting on righteousness as a breastplate and an helmet of salvation upon His head; Isaiah 11:5 girds Messiah's loins with righteousness and faithfulness; Isaiah 52:7 has the feet shod with the gospel of peace. Paul is dressing the believer in God's own kit. So the breastplate is not the Christian's righteousness but the righteousness of God in Christ, the belt is truth rather than sincerity, and the shield is faith — which is reliance on Someone else — rather than resolve. A soldier who has to manufacture his own armour has none.

The proportion of the kit is instructive: five pieces of defence and one weapon, and the weapon is the word of God. Nothing in the list is a technique, a formula or a spiritual exercise. The list ends, in verse 18, with praying always with all prayer and supplication in the Spirit — not a seventh piece but the posture in which the armour is worn. A church that has turned the passage into a checklist of practices to perform each morning has kept the vocabulary and lost the thing, which is a man standing in what God supplies, asking Him for more.

Romans 13:12 names the same equipment the armour of light and sets it against the works of darkness, and the setting is the night far spent and the day at hand. That is the eschatology under the armour: it is worn by people who know what time it is. First Thessalonians 5:8 says the same — let us, who are of the day, be sober, putting on the breastplate. Watchfulness and sobriety are the disposition; the pieces are given to the watchful. The evil day of Ephesians 6:13 is not a rumour but a scheduled engagement, and the passage's confidence is that the kit will hold.
roots_summary: Greek panoplia (G3833), whole armour, full kit; thorax (G2382), breastplate; perikephalaia (G4030), helmet; machaira tou pneumatos (G3162), the sword of the Spirit.
roots_lines: Greek panoplia tou theou (G3833) — the whole armour of God; Ephesians 6:11, 6:13; also Luke 11:22.
Greek hopla tou photos (G3696, G5457) — the armour of light; Romans 13:12; hopla dikaiosunes, 2 Corinthians 6:7.
usage: “The whole armour of God” — and Isaiah shows Him wearing it.
“And having done all, to stand” — five pieces of defence, one weapon.
“Praying always” — the posture the armour is worn in, verse 18.

pos: n. phrase (the two lepta a poor widow put in the temple treasury, which the Lord weighed above all the rest)
etymology: Greek lepton, the thin one — the smallest coin in circulation; two made a kodrantes, a Roman quadrans, which Mark translates for his readers. English mite was a small Flemish copper coin, chosen by the translators as the nearest thing to nothing.
biblical_def: The widow's mite is observed from a seat opposite the treasury: “Jesus sat over against the treasury, and beheld how the people cast money into the treasury: and many that were rich cast in much” (Mar 12:41). “And there came a certain poor widow, and she threw in two mites, which make a farthing” (Mar 12:42). The verdict reverses the arithmetic: “this poor widow hath cast more in, than all they which have cast into the treasury” (Mar 12:43), and the reason is proportion: “all they did cast in of their abundance; but she of her want did cast in all that she had, even all her living” (Mar 12:44). Paul states the rule: “if there be first a willing mind, it is accepted according to that a man hath, and not according to that he hath not” (2Co 8:12).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines mite as a small coin, formerly current in England, a third of a farthing; and, from the Scripture, a very small quantity or particle, as of money; a small weight; and observes that the widow's mite is proverbial for a small gift from the poor.
webster_full: MITE, n. A small weight; the twentieth part of a grain.
2. Any thing proverbially very small; a very little particle or quantity.
3. A small coin, formerly current in England, being about a third of a farthing.
The widow's mite. Mark 12.
scriptures: And Jesus sat over against the treasury, and beheld how the people cast money into the treasury: and many that were rich cast in much.
And there came a certain poor widow, and she threw in two mites, which make a farthing.
And he called unto him his disciples, and saith unto them, Verily I say unto you, That this poor widow hath cast more in, than all they which have cast into the treasury:
For all they did cast in of their abundance; but she of her want did cast in all that she had, even all her living.
For if there be first a willing mind, it is accepted according to that a man hath, and not according to that he hath not.
corruption_summary: The story is used to press the poor for more, and the verse before it condemns men who devour widows' houses.
corruption_paragraphs: Mark 12:40 is the sentence immediately before the widow enters, and it is never read at the offering. The Lord has just described the scribes which devour widows' houses, and for a pretence make long prayers, and said they shall receive greater damnation. Then He sits down opposite the treasury and watches a widow put in her whole living. The two scenes are one scene. Whatever else the passage is, it is an observation of a religious system that had taught a destitute woman to give it everything she had, and the Lord's next words, in chapter 13, are that not one stone of that temple would be left upon another.

That does not cancel the commendation, and the church has rightly heard one. She gave more than all of them — the Lord says so, and the measure He uses is stated: they gave of their abundance, she of her want. The arithmetic of heaven is proportional, not absolute, which is the rule Paul lays down in 2 Corinthians 8:12 — accepted according to that a man hath. That is a comfort to the poor and a rebuke to the rich in the same clause. A large gift that cost nothing is weighed at nothing, and the widow's two coins were the heaviest thing put in that box.

The passage is also a warning about who does the weighing. Nobody in the temple court noticed the widow; the rich gave visibly and much, which is what treasuries are designed to register. Jesus sat and beheld how — not how much, but how — and called the disciples over to explain what they had missed. The doctrine of the passage is that the Lord watches giving from a seat where the amounts are visible and the proportions are what count, and that He sees the two mites go in. What a church does with that knowledge in its appeals is a matter of whether it stands with the scribes or with Him.
roots_summary: Greek lepton (G3016), a mite, the thin coin; kodrantes (G2835), a farthing, quadrans; gazophulakion (G1049), the treasury; husteresis (G5304), want, poverty.
roots_lines: Greek lepta duo (G3016) — two mites; Mark 12:42, Luke 21:2; also Luke 12:59.
Greek ek tes hustereseos autes (G5304) — of her want; Mark 12:44, and Philippians 4:11 of Paul's.
usage: “Which devour widows' houses” — the verse before she enters.
“Of her want did cast in all that she had” — the arithmetic is proportional.
“Beheld how the people cast” — how, not how much.

pos: n. phrase (Israel's forty years and Christ's forty days — the proving of a people and of a Son in the place where there is nothing to lean on)
etymology: Hebrew midbar, the uninhabited land, and nasah, to test or prove — the word for assaying metal; Greek peirazo, which the AV renders both tempt and try. The same word describes the devil's work and God's, and the difference is the purpose.
biblical_def: Wilderness testing is explained by Moses at the end of it: “thou shalt remember all the way which the LORD thy God led thee these forty years in the wilderness, to humble thee, and to prove thee, to know what was in thine heart, whether thou wouldest keep his commandments, or no” (Deu 8:2). Its lesson is stated: “that he might make thee know that man doth not live by bread only, but by every word that proceedeth out of the mouth of the LORD” (Deu 8:3). Christ repeats the course: “Then was Jesus led up of the Spirit into the wilderness to be tempted of the devil” (Mat 4:1), and answers from that lesson: “It is written, Man shall not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceedeth out of the mouth of God” (Mat 4:4). And the church is warned not to repeat the failure: “Harden not your hearts, as in the provocation, in the day of temptation in the wilderness” (Heb 3:8).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines wilderness as a desert, a tract of land or region uncultivated and uninhabited by human beings; and, in Scripture, the deserts of Arabia through which Israel passed; and to prove as to try, to ascertain some unknown quality by an experiment, or by a standard.
webster_full: WILDERNESS, n. A desert; a tract of land or region uncultivated and uninhabited by human beings, whether a forest or a wide barren plain.
In the United States, it is applied only to a forest. In Scripture, it is applied frequently to the deserts of Arabia.
PROVE, v.t. To try; to ascertain some unknown quality or truth by an experiment, or by a test or standard.
2. To evince, establish or ascertain as truth, reality or fact, by testimony or other evidence.
3. To experience; to try by suffering or encountering.
scriptures: Deu 8:2

And thou shalt remember all the way which the LORD thy God led thee these forty years in the wilderness, to humble thee, and to prove thee, to know what was in thine heart, whether thou wouldest keep his commandments, or no.
Deu 8:3

And he humbled thee, and suffered thee to hunger, and fed thee with manna, which thou knewest not, neither did thy fathers know; that he might make thee know that man doth not live by bread only, but by every word that proceedeth out of the mouth of the LORD doth man live.
Mat 4:1
Then was Jesus led up of the Spirit into the wilderness to be tempted of the devil.
Mat 4:4
But he answered and said, It is written, Man shall not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceedeth out of the mouth of God.
Heb 3:8
Harden not your hearts, as in the provocation, in the day of temptation in the wilderness:
corruption_summary: The wilderness is read as punishment, and Deuteronomy says its purpose was to humble, to prove, and to teach a people what they lived on.
corruption_paragraphs: Deuteronomy 8:2 gives three purposes and none of them is punishment. The forty years were to humble, to prove, and to know what was in thine heart — not for God's information but for Israel's, since a heart's contents are discovered under pressure and nowhere else. The wilderness is where the props are gone: no field, no cistern, no wall. What a man leans on when there is nothing to lean on is what he actually trusts, and the desert was the instrument for finding out. A believer in a stripped season should hear that verse before he hears any other.

Matthew 4 is Israel's forty years compressed into forty days and passed. The Spirit leads Jesus into the wilderness — the same Spirit, the same word led that Deuteronomy uses of Israel — and each of the three temptations is answered from Deuteronomy 6 to 8, the chapters about Israel's testing. Where Israel demanded bread, He would not make it; where Israel tested God at Massah, He would not; where Israel bowed to a calf, He would not bow. He is the Son who kept the course the son had failed, and Hebrews says He was tempted in all points like as we are, yet without sin — which means He knows the desert from inside and not as a spectator.

Hebrews 3 turns the history on the church and it is uncomfortable. The provocation in the wilderness is quoted as a present-tense warning: to day, if ye will hear his voice, harden not your hearts. The people who saw the sea part and ate the manna are the ones who fell in the desert, because they saw His works forty years and did not learn His ways. Having been delivered does not settle the matter; the testing comes after the Red Sea, not before it, and the writer's fear for his readers is that they have the exodus and not the land.
roots_summary: Hebrew midbar (H4057), wilderness; nasah (H5254), to test, prove; anah (H6031), to humble, afflict; Greek peirazo (G3985), to tempt, try.
roots_lines: Hebrew nasah (H5254) — to prove, test; Deuteronomy 8:2, 8:16, Exodus 16:4, 20:20, and of Israel testing God, Exodus 17:2, 17:7.
Greek peirazo (G3985) — to tempt, put to the test; Matthew 4:1, Hebrews 2:18, 3:9, 4:15.
usage: “To know what was in thine heart” — discovered under pressure, nowhere else.
“Then was Jesus led up of the Spirit into the wilderness” — the same course, passed.
“As in the provocation” — the testing comes after the Red Sea.

pos: n. phrase (the song of heaven in Revelation 5; the sevenfold ascription to the Lamb that was slain)
etymology: Greek arnion, a little lamb — the diminutive, used twenty-nine times in Revelation and once elsewhere, and axios, worthy, of due weight. The One who governs the book is named by the smallest and most defenceless word available.
biblical_def: Worthy is the Lamb is sung by every creature: “Worthy is the Lamb that was slain to receive power, and riches, and wisdom, and strength, and honour, and glory, and blessing” (Rev 5:12). The ground of the worthiness is given first: “Thou art worthy to take the book, and to open the seals thereof: for thou wast slain, and hast redeemed us to God by thy blood” (Rev 5:9). The Lamb is seen before He is sung: “in the midst of the throne… stood a Lamb as it had been slain, having seven horns and seven eyes” (Rev 5:6). The title was given at the Jordan: “Behold the Lamb of God, which taketh away the sin of the world” (John 1:29). And Isaiah saw the slaughter: “he is brought as a lamb to the slaughter, and as a sheep before her shearers is dumb, so he openeth not his mouth” (Isa 53:7).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines lamb as the young of the sheep kind, and, in Scripture, the Lamb of God, the Savior Jesus Christ, who was offered as a sacrifice for sins; and worthy as deserving, having merit, possessing worth or excellence of qualities.
webster_full: LAMB, n. The young of the sheep kind.
2. The Lamb of God, in Scripture, the Savior Jesus Christ, who was typified by the paschal lamb.
Behold the Lamb of God, who taketh away the sin of the world. John 1.
WORTHY, a. Deserving; such as merits; having worth or excellence; as a worthy man.
2. Possessing worth or excellence of qualities; virtuous; estimable.
scriptures: Rev 5:12
Saying with a loud voice, Worthy is the Lamb that was slain to receive power, and riches, and wisdom, and strength, and honour, and glory, and blessing.
Rev 5:9

And they sung a new song, saying, Thou art worthy to take the book, and to open the seals thereof: for thou wast slain, and hast redeemed us to God by thy blood out of every kindred, and tongue, and people, and nation;
Rev 5:6

And I beheld, and, lo, in the midst of the throne and of the four beasts, and in the midst of the elders, stood a Lamb as it had been slain, having seven horns and seven eyes, which are the seven Spirits of God sent forth into all the earth.
John 1:29
The next day John seeth Jesus coming unto him, and saith, Behold the Lamb of God, which taketh away the sin of the world.
Isa 53:7
He was oppressed, and he was afflicted, yet he opened not his mouth: he is brought as a lamb to the slaughter, and as a sheep before her shearers is dumb, so he openeth not his mouth.
corruption_summary: The Lamb is sung as gentle and nothing more, and the Lamb of Revelation opens the seals, has seven horns, and has a wrath the kings flee from.
corruption_paragraphs: The word is a diminutive — a little lamb — and the figure in Revelation 5:6 is as it had been slain, standing with the marks of its death on it. That is the meekness the church rightly sings. But the same verse gives the Lamb seven horns and seven eyes, which are complete power and complete sight; the Lamb opens the seals that release judgment; and in chapter 6 the kings of the earth call on the mountains to hide them from the wrath of the Lamb. A Lamb with wrath is a deliberate paradox and the book will not let either half go. The slain One is the One in authority, and the authority is exercised by the slain One.

The song grounds the worthiness in a purchase, and the grounding matters for theology. Chapter 4 sings Thou art worthy, O Lord, to receive glory and honour and power: for thou hast created all things — the Creator's worthiness. Chapter 5 sings Thou art worthy to take the book… for thou wast slain, and hast redeemed us to God by thy blood — the Redeemer's. The Lamb is not worthy merely because He is divine; He is worthy to open history because He paid for it. That is why 5:12 heaps up seven things — power, riches, wisdom, strength, honour, glory, blessing — the number of completeness, as if the singers were emptying the vocabulary.

Isaiah 53:7 and John 1:29 stand behind the song and supply its silence. The lamb brought to the slaughter openeth not his mouth; the Lamb of God taketh away the sin of the world, in a present tense that the church has been living inside ever since. Revelation 5 is the only place in Scripture where every creature in heaven and on earth and under the sea is heard at once, and what they agree on is the worth of the One who did not defend Himself. The church's whole liturgy, every Lord's day, is a rehearsal of that verse by a choir still learning its part.
roots_summary: Greek arnion (G721), a little lamb; axios (G514), worthy, of weight; esphagmenon (G4969), slain, slaughtered; Hebrew seh (H7716), a lamb, one of the flock.
roots_lines: Greek arnion (G721) — little lamb; Revelation 5:6–13, 6:16, 7:17, 21:23, 22:3; elsewhere only John 21:15.
Greek hos esphagmenon (G4969) — as it had been slain; Revelation 5:6, 5:9, 5:12, 13:8.
Hebrew kasseh lattebach (H7716, H2874) — as a lamb to the slaughter; Isaiah 53:7, Jeremiah 11:19.
usage: “A Lamb as it had been slain, having seven horns” — the paradox the book keeps.
“For thou wast slain” — the Redeemer's worthiness, after the Creator's.
“Power, and riches, and wisdom, and strength, and honour, and glory, and blessing” — seven.
